name: Moore's Law

claims.claim_text: Fabs pursue each process generation under competitive pressure rather than choice: if one company does not advance the node, a competitor will, which is why the whole industry marches in step.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're just marching along thanks to Moore's Law. You know, they're doing what they have to do because if they didn't, someone else would. And, you know, and a lot of the other fabs are doing that now too. They're working on FinFets is another one.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Contests, Ham Radio & TWIT.tv - Ham, Spam, Thank You Ma'am

claims.claim_text: The scaling trend is usually quoted as a doubling every 18 months, but the underlying statement is about how much silicon function fits in the same area at the same price, not about processor speed.
claims.quote_verbatim: It has to double every 18 months for the Moore's Law.
claims.episode_title: EE Movies, Part Rants and SPICE.

claims.claim_text: New architectural techniques such as parallelism can deliver performance gains that run ahead of the process-scaling schedule, so system performance and transistor scaling are separable.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know, you can come up with new architecture technology and stuff like that actually ahead of that schedule. So, I guess, yeah, you can churn out, you know, processors twice as quick as Moore's Law or something.
claims.episode_title: EE Movies, Part Rants and SPICE.

claims.claim_text: A common design habit is to accept slow compute-heavy tools on the assumption that future process generations will make them fast enough, deferring optimization work indefinitely.
claims.quote_verbatim: It takes a lot of, a lot of processing to do that stuff. But man, it's, that's crazy. But that'll be taken care of by Moore's Law. So no problem. Yeah. Just keep waiting.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: CAD programs, Systems Design and Renewable Energy

claims.claim_text: Extrapolating exponential doubling to the physical limit of one bit per atom gives an absolute ceiling of roughly 600 years, after which all reachable matter would be consumed as storage.
claims.quote_verbatim: And he did a calculation based on Moore's Law. It has a lifetime of 600 years. Beyond that, basically, every atom in the near light universe will be consumed by data.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Innovation Speculation

claims.claim_text: One widely circulated forecast placed the breakdown of transistor scaling in the 2020 to 2030 window.
claims.quote_verbatim: the breakdown of Moore's Law, which I think he's predicting is going to be in the 2020 to 2030
claims.episode_title: Moore's Law, GaN and SiC devices - Gallimaufry GaN Gabble

claims.claim_text: When scaling stops, memory capacity per generation stops multiplying, removing the yearly spec jump manufacturers had relied on for new product cycles.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because, you know, scaling won't work anymore. You won't be able to get ten times the memory, you know, next year that you had a couple years before.
claims.episode_title: Moore's Law, GaN and SiC devices - Gallimaufry GaN Gabble

claims.claim_text: Clock frequency stopped being the competitive axis once desktop processors sat near three gigahertz for over a decade, ending the megahertz race well before density scaling stopped.
claims.quote_verbatim: he started the talk basically saying that computers have been at three gigahertz for over a decade now, right? Like, computers have been at three gig for a long time.
claims.episode_title: Moore's Law, GaN and SiC devices - Gallimaufry GaN Gabble

claims.claim_text: Large corporations pipeline product development around the process cadence, so each year's product is far enough ahead that an individual builder cannot match it.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can work so quickly, and they pipeline their product development such that they worked with Moore's Law basically to their advantage
claims.episode_title: Moore's Law, GaN and SiC devices - Gallimaufry GaN Gabble

claims.claim_text: A better strategy for a small hardware business than waiting for scaling to stall is to target niches large corporations serve badly.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of waiting for Moore's Law to crap out, perhaps it's a better idea to just try to position yourself in the industries that big corporations are not good at servicing
claims.episode_title: Moore's Law, GaN and SiC devices - Gallimaufry GaN Gabble

claims.claim_text: Backward compatibility plus steady process gains makes incremental speedups the rational business choice, which suppresses architectural risk-taking such as moving the processor next to the memory.
claims.quote_verbatim: backward compatibility, running your code that you have today and just trying to, you know, turn the crank on Moore's law and just get the process a little faster. I mean, that is just, I mean, it just totally makes business sense.
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: Fast process cadence compresses innovation into a window of months, because a full-stack idea must show a compelling improvement before the next node makes it irrelevant.
claims.quote_verbatim: Moore's law has sort of compressed innovation into this very narrow window of time where essentially you have to do the whole stack within, you know, months these days, maybe years at best
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: Physics makes the slowdown of transistor scaling essentially inevitable, and longer cycle times then give architectural ideas more room to prove viability.
claims.quote_verbatim: the slowdown of Moore's law is, um, relatively inevitable in my opinion, um, because there's physics and that's going to slow things down.
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: When a process node runs out of headroom, effort shifts to packaging improvements until packaging itself becomes the limiting factor and a new node jump is made.
claims.quote_verbatim: when they run out of silicon stuff on a node, when they run out of, run out of juice, they start looking at packaging until they finally make a jump and the packaging becomes a limiting factor then.
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: If hardware performance stays flat for years, multi-year investments in optimizing compilers and hand-coded assembly start paying off because the gains are not erased by the next chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: hand, hand coded assembly routines actually start making sense now because you get, you know, big performance gains out of it.
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: The industry has largely moved to a fabless-plus-foundry structure, with Intel the prime remaining example of a vertically integrated device manufacturer.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've very much gone to a foundry model by and large, there are very few completely vertically integrated companies anymore, Intel being the prime example of a still vertically integrated device manufacturer.
claims.speaker: Steve Leibson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Steve Leibson - Impavid Ideopraxist Insider

claims.claim_text: At 28 and 20 nanometers the process physics is severe enough that EDA tool selection can no longer be separated from the choice of foundry, forcing collaboration and heavy mathematical modeling.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't really divorce the tool acquisition from going to the foundry anymore. It's becoming far more collaborative because the physics of what's happening at 28 and 20 nanometers is ferocious.
claims.speaker: Steve Leibson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Steve Leibson - Impavid Ideopraxist Insider

claims.claim_text: Logic was bipolar until around 1980 and was abandoned not because it stopped getting faster but because its power dissipation became intolerable, which is what drove the switch to CMOS.
claims.quote_verbatim: We were going to go with bipolar forever because it got faster and faster and faster. And we didn't quite notice, but it also got hotter and hotter and hotter and hotter.
claims.speaker: Steve Leibson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Steve Leibson - Impavid Ideopraxist Insider

claims.claim_text: Companies betting on gallium arsenide for speed lost out because CMOS became fast enough, a recurring pattern where an incumbent process outruns an exotic alternative.
claims.quote_verbatim: the companies that were counting on doing things in like gallium arsenide, they fell by the wayside because CMOS got fast enough.
claims.speaker: Steve Leibson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Steve Leibson - Impavid Ideopraxist Insider

claims.claim_text: An IBM semiconductor R&D leader estimated on a DAC panel that conventional semiconductor technology had about two more decades of runway.
claims.quote_verbatim: he gave semiconductor technology another two decades to run
claims.speaker: Steve Leibson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Steve Leibson - Impavid Ideopraxist Insider

claims.claim_text: The scaling trend functions as a self-fulfilling prophecy rather than a physical law: each company invests to keep it on schedule because a competitor otherwise will.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know that if you do not invest in making Moore's Law happen, that the guy down the street or the guy across the ocean will.
claims.speaker: Steve Leibson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Steve Leibson - Impavid Ideopraxist Insider

claims.claim_text: Commodity ARM cores driven by smartphone volume became powerful enough that custom hardware such as FPGAs stopped being necessary for many embedded control applications.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's just so much power coming out from these kind of standard platforms that we don't really see the need for custom hardware. It's just the kind of commodity hardware is just getting so good so fast.
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Analog preprocessing before conversion has real niches at low power, low amplitude and low sensitivity, but analog will not match digital scaling for integration, complexity and processing throughput.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't think analog's ever gonna beat, uh, Moore's law in terms of integration and complexity and, and processing power.
claims.speaker: Kent Lundberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Kent Lundberg - Luculent Linear Legacy

claims.claim_text: Using the chessboard-and-rice doubling parable, the counted generations of technology doubling passed the 32nd square around 2006, the point where an exponential becomes visibly overwhelming.
claims.quote_verbatim: and the 32nd square in terms of generations of doublings actually happened in 2006
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Guns and Mobile Labs - Nuanced Nomadic Non-essentials

claims.claim_text: CMOS scaling continues because demand for storage, processing and lower power funds it; without that economic pull the technical progress would stop regardless of physics.
claims.quote_verbatim: So they keep scaling CMOS aggressively because there's a lot of money driving it. If you remove the driving behind it, obviously nothing will happen.
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shahriar from The Signal Path - Quisquous Quivering Quadripole

claims.claim_text: Around eight nanometer device dimensions CMOS is expected to need a fundamentally different approach, though that boundary has been predicted for roughly a decade without arriving.
claims.quote_verbatim: even with CMOS too, once you hit about eight nanometer devices and you have to perhaps do something different. Although people have been saying this for, I don't know, 10 years.
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shahriar from The Signal Path - Quisquous Quivering Quadripole

claims.claim_text: Bond pads do not shrink at anything like the rate transistors do, so on advanced nodes a small die becomes pad limited rather than transistor limited.
claims.quote_verbatim: you are getting to the point where you might become pad limited because pads don't shrink nearly as fast as transistors shrink in Moore's law
claims.speaker: Luke Beno
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Luke Beno of Analog.io

claims.claim_text: Falling digital electronics cost reset test equipment pricing: an entry-level benchtop scope sat near 800 dollars for decades until Rigol halved the 1052E price to 400 dollars in 2009.
claims.quote_verbatim: They cut the price of the 1052e from 800 bucks to 400 bucks.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Call In Show #4

claims.claim_text: Process headroom running out revived interest in programmable logic, restoring the long-standing tradeoff between FPGA custom logic and brute-force parallel processors.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was kind of like the FPGA versus, you know, just raw cyclical processing and stuff. That's kind of been the trade-off for a long time.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Gotta Update My Dog

claims.claim_text: Once density gains in the plane stall, the industry response is vertical stacking of die, the same move a densely populated area makes when land runs out.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of increasing the area or reducing the size, they're doing what they're doing, they're going to start going to stacking the chips. It's just like a densely populated area once you run out of...
claims.speaker: Jake Baker
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jake Baker

claims.claim_text: Whether the scaling trend is over depends on which definition is used: the lithographic shrink-and-double reading versus the macro reading of memory halving in price and doubling in capacity every nine to eighteen months.
claims.quote_verbatim: Do you look at Moore's Law from a, just a, you know, a photographic, you know, process kind of thing of shrinking things down and doubling, or do you look at it as a macro thing?
claims.speaker: Jake Baker
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jake Baker

claims.claim_text: The historical default answer to a performance shortfall was to wait roughly 18 months for faster silicon; when that stops working, the remaining lever is spending engineering time optimizing code or turning it into dedicated hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: You wait 18 months and you get the new set of chips in and Moore's law has taken care of you. If we start running out of that, then, you know, the thing that's going to get us more efficiencies is spending more time optimizing code
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: A Decoupled Episode

claims.claim_text: GlobalFoundries halting seven nanometer development was a single-company capability decision, not an industry ceiling, since TSMC continued developing that node.
claims.quote_verbatim: the global foundry stopping seven nanometer development that is not the that is a misleading title because i thought it was like nobody's going to hit seven nanometers it's like well tsmc is still doing their thing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Nerds In A Corner

claims.claim_text: Slowing process gains increased interest in open source FPGA toolchains, because optimizing custom logic becomes worthwhile when free performance no longer arrives.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think that that's getting a lot of traction because of the slowing of Moore's Law, sloring slash stopping of Moore's Law in the first place. That more people are actually interested in optimizing custom logic
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Legend of Keyzermas

claims.claim_text: Plotting released processor transistor counts against the predicted doubling line shows the actual data oscillating ahead of and behind the trend rather than following it smoothly.
claims.quote_verbatim: they chart the, the transistor count of different processors and run into the released and it tracks, like it basically is like, it goes ahead a little bit and then it tracks back and it goes ahead and back and back and forth.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Man Behind The Curtain

claims.claim_text: The trend is commonly stated as a doubling of transistors every 18 to 24 months, and its author co-founded the company named for integrated electronics that produced the first single-chip microprocessor.
claims.quote_verbatim: doubling of transistors every 18 to 24 months, you know, knowing that he was a founder of a company that's still around today and made the first, uh, microprocessor on a single chip
claims.speaker: Brock LaMeres
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brock LaMeres

claims.claim_text: Chiplet and heterogeneous system integration is positioned as the successor enabler for semiconductor innovation as monolithic scaling reaches its end.
claims.quote_verbatim: chiplet integration or heterogeneous system integration, is the future of semiconductor industry. It is fundamentally going to be the enabler of any new innovation because Moore's law is probably coming to an end
claims.speaker: Ming Zhang
claims.episode_title: Discussing Chiplets with Ming Zhang

claims.claim_text: Proprietary process design kits carry legal overhead measured in 800-dollar-per-hour lawyer time, so only ideas the team is already confident in get explored; open PDKs lower that barrier to trying speculative architectures.
claims.quote_verbatim: This means that only ideas which people are extremely confident about actually get explored, right?
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Transistor count per chip has kept roughly doubling while what changed is how the transistors are usable: single-threaded performance hit a ceiling and core counts rose instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: the traditional, um, specification of Moore's law around transistors is still actually somewhat surviving. The number of transistors every year is doubling. Um, but how those transistors are being used and how they can take a benefit of them has been changing. We've kind of hit the ceiling in single threaded performance.
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Clock frequency stopped being a marketing spec after the megahertz and gigahertz races of the 1990s, replaced by core count as the headline number.
claims.quote_verbatim: nobody advertises a CPU on gigahertz these days. Right. Um, uh, back in the 1990s, there was always the gigahertz war or like the megahertz wars back then
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Adding cores only helps if memory bandwidth can feed them, and packing more transistors into a small area raises power density and makes heat extraction a serious limit.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have this many cores, you need the memory bandwidth to feed it. Um, and how do you get the data in and out fast enough? So those cores aren't sitting there unused.
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: ASIC design methodology has not been rethought at 100x scale increments the way software practice has; chips are still designed with late-1990s methods because process scaling supplied the speed gains instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: We're still designing a lot of these, um, CPUs and chips and stuff using, uh, a lot of the same ideas and methodologies that we were back in, you know, the late 1990s. And we've just kind of relied on Moore's law to enable us to get faster.
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: FPGAs give software-style deployment timescales, worldwide in minutes rather than years, but pay a substantial silicon cost for that configurability.
claims.quote_verbatim: FPGAs give a software style deployment, I can deploy worldwide in, you know, minutes instead of years. Um, and the thing is though, that FPGAs pay a pretty high cost for that configurability.
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: The trend states that chip density doubles roughly every 18 months, not that chips double in speed; the speed reading is a common misquote.
claims.quote_verbatim: people think that Moore's law says that chips get, you know, what chips double in speed every, uh, every 18 months, but that's not true. It's chip density doubles every 18 months.
claims.episode_title: Finishing Prototypes with Zack Freedman

claims.claim_text: Extra density can be spent three different ways at the manufacturer's discretion: more speed, lower power for battery life, or more parts per wafer at the same die function.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it's up to the manufacturer, whether they want to use that, those extras, whether they want to use that extra power to double the speed or to have the battery consumption or to make, uh, or to make 50% more on, you know, with the same piece of Silicon.
claims.episode_title: Finishing Prototypes with Zack Freedman

claims.claim_text: As the density curve flattened, a counterpart cost curve moved the opposite way, with semiconductor development cost rising as dimensions shrink.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is moresla thing that is kind of flattened out and then there is the another equivalent of it that describes that the cost of semiconductors also goes up in the opposite direction
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: Debunking with Shahriar

claims.claim_text: Below the wavelength limit of deep UV lithography, a single layer is decomposed into several coarser patterns that are exposed on top of one another to reach the fine resolution, a technique called multiple patterning.
claims.quote_verbatim: and then they they multiple pattern expose them on top of each other so to get the fine resolution
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: Debunking with Shahriar

claims.claim_text: Multiple patterning removes layout freedom that older nodes allowed: gates can no longer be placed at arbitrary orientations and everything on a layer must run the same direction.
claims.quote_verbatim: you used to be able to put your devices in any orientation you wanted you could have the gates going in zero degrees like that oh this is orientation dependent really but now you can't do that anymore because of the patterning limitations everything has to be the same direction
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: Debunking with Shahriar

claims.claim_text: Only about two or three companies worldwide can run five and three nanometer CMOS processes, namely TSMC and Samsung with Intel potentially reaching them.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's actually like if i think there's only maybe two or three semiconductor companies now in the world that can do these five three kind of nanometer process in the tsmc and samsung intel potentially could get there
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: Debunking with Shahriar

claims.claim_text: High-speed RF parts are typically not built on leading-edge CMOS but on silicon germanium BiCMOS, where SiGe bipolar devices provide higher breakdown for power handling and the on-die CMOS is a far older node used as a helper.
claims.quote_verbatim: silicon germanium is a device with a higher breakdown so you can create high power devices and it's a different different beast altogether
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: Debunking with Shahriar

claims.claim_text: Node advancement is driven by commercial survival rather than technical enthusiasm; engineers inside the chip industry describe the work as a grind sustained by competitive necessity.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not, people aren't doubling their transistor count every 18 months or whatever it's actually doing these days. Uh, you know, it's not because of, because it's fun to make things smaller.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pavlovian Cheapskates

claims.claim_text: The long-run trend in cost of compute is downward toward zero, now driven by GPUs, TPUs and algorithmic efficiency rather than transistor scaling alone, letting models that needed a cluster run on local machines.
claims.quote_verbatim: as a trend, right, the cost of compute is going to zero. Over time, right? Like if you look at kind of like, you know, just Moore's law over the last 40 years, but now what GPUs and TPUs and, you know, and just like more and more intelligent algorithms are doing.
claims.speaker: Sergiy Nesterenko
claims.episode_title: Intelligent Routing with Sergiy Nesterenko

claims.claim_text: Integrating everything onto one monolithic die is the performance-optimal answer, giving roughly 13 metal layers, hundred-nanometer wire pitches, and the best energy efficiency, cost and bandwidth.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's the performance optimal version. Cause then you get like 13 layers of metal, the distances can probably be in the hundreds of microns.
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: Accessible ASICs with Andreas Olofsson

claims.claim_text: Monolithic integration trades away modularity entirely: each chip becomes a statically compiled blob with no reuse, whereas chiplets give hardware the equivalent of software libraries and linking.
claims.quote_verbatim: the energy efficiency, the cost, the bandwidth, everything is awesome, but you get no modularity, right? You basically compile one function into one thing and it has zero reuse factor
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: Accessible ASICs with Andreas Olofsson

claims.claim_text: The end of easy gains in general purpose computing opens more silicon niches, making specialized chip startups more viable than during the era of uniform scaling.
claims.quote_verbatim: we will see more Silicon startups, especially now with like more niches available and kind of the end of the gains of Moore's law and general purpose computing
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: Modern node names are marketing labels rather than feature sizes: a so-called two nanometer node contains no two nanometer features, and physics limits real dimensions to roughly ten or eleven nanometers.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's kind of like they talk about the two nanometer CMOS node, but the truth be known is you really can't go below. I think it's 10 or 11 nanometers due to physics.
claims.speaker: Jerry Twomey
claims.episode_title: Applied Embedded Electronics with Jerry Twomey

claims.claim_text: After roughly 40 years of hard scaling, present-day improvements come from more parallel processing rather than smaller transistors, and no successor with comparable breadth of application has emerged.
claims.quote_verbatim: the way people are improving things is they're not improving things with smaller transistors. They're more improving things with more parallel processing.
claims.speaker: Jerry Twomey
claims.episode_title: Applied Embedded Electronics with Jerry Twomey

claims.claim_text: Efficiency was historically bought by lowering supply rails alongside parallelization, but rail voltages have approached diode drop levels, removing that lever.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were driving up efficiency by driving down power rails in the past as well. So parallelization, lower voltages, but we're just like, we've approached diode voltages
claims.episode_title: Applied Embedded Electronics with Jerry Twomey

claims.claim_text: Current compute scaling is limited by power and by DRAM cost rather than by lithography alone, pushing gains toward efficiency instead of raw capability.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think we're reaching some power limits and obviously some scaling limits, thanks to the DRAM makers and this cost DRAM
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: AI Tooling with Matt Liberty and Luke Beno

claims.claim_text: Very large scale integration is what makes modern phased arrays practical, supplying the many data converters and wide data pipes that mechanically scanned radar could not.
claims.quote_verbatim: we can have lots of data converters and, and Y data pipes, thanks to the very large scale integration, right? We're so-called the riding of Moore's law. Well, that's a very real thing.
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: The Terahertz Frontier with Greg Charvat of Teradar

attribution_notes: Episode 17: the two passages overlap and the transcript alternates Chris Gammell / Dave Jones labels mid-exchange, so the speaker of the 'silicon in the same area for the same price' definition cannot be resolved; left null.

Passage [18] is labeled Chris Gammell and the opening question voice is the interviewer, so the cheap-chips claim is attributed to Chris Gammell.
Episode 99: labeled 'Steve Liebson'; normalized to the guest's name Steve Leibson since the content is his own foundry/EDA panel experience.

Episode 297: passages [30]-[32] are labeled Dave Jones, but the content is the guest answering questions about chip stacking and node teaching from his own design experience; attributed to Jake Baker. Passage [33] is labeled Chris Gammell and reads as the interviewer's question plus the guest's answer, so the teaching claim is attributed to Jake Baker as well.
Episode 499 is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE; the chiplet claim is first-person guest content about his own view of heterogeneous integration, so Ming Zhang is used.
Episode 650 is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE; the monolithic-versus-chiplet explanation is the guest answering a direct question with his own ASIC background, so Andreas Olofsson is used.
Episode 550: labeled Chris Gammell, but the density-versus-speed explanation could belong to either host or guest Zack Freedman; left null.
Episode 553: labeled 'Shahriar Shahramian' with guest field 'Shahriar Faramian'; content is his own RF/silicon-germanium process experience, so Shahriar Shahramian is used.

Episode 704: the passage is labeled Dave Jones but contains both guest Jerry Twomey's first-person answers and an interviewer follow-up about power rails. Twomey's own statements are attributed to him; the power-rail follow-up is left null.
